source_refs.note: Book p. 90-93: 3.5 Integration by Using Partial Fractions; Case-I to Case-IV boxes; Examples 40-43

blocks.text: If \(P(x)\), \(Q(x)\) are polynomial functions and the denominator \(Q(x)\ (x \ne 0)\), in the rational function \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\), can be factorized into linear and quadratic (irreducible) factors, then the rational function \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) is written as a sum of simpler rational functions, each of which can be integrated by methods already known to us.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the condition as \(Q(x)\ (x \ne 0)\). The condition is on the denominator, not on \(x\): it should read \(Q(x) \ne 0\) (the fraction is defined only where the denominator is not zero).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why do we need this method? Integrals such as \(\int \frac{dx}{x - 2}\) or \(\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}\) are easy, but \(\int \frac{3x - 2}{x(x - 1)(x - 2)}\,dx\) has no ready formula. Partial fractions reverse the process of adding fractions: we break one hard fraction into a sum of easy fractions (you met partial fractions in Class XI), and then integrate each easy fraction.
Before you start, check two things:
1. Is the fraction proper (degree of \(P\) less than degree of \(Q\))? If not, divide first: \(\frac{P}{Q} = \text{quotient} + \frac{\text{remainder}}{Q}\).
2. Is \(Q(x)\) fully factorised into linear factors and irreducible quadratic factors? A quadratic \(ax^2 + bx + c\) is irreducible when \(b^2 - 4ac < 0\).
Here, we will give examples of the following four cases when the denominator \(Q(x)\) contains

items: Case-II: Repeated and non-repeated linear factors.
Case-III: Linear and non repeated irreducible quadratic factors.
Case-IV: Linear and repeated irreducible quadratic factors.

rows: \(\frac{Ax + B}{x^2 + bx + c} + \frac{Cx + D}{(x^2 + bx + c)^2}\)
blocks.caption: Our summary table: which partial fractions each kind of factor needs

blocks.title: Teaching note
Case-I
blocks.text: Integration of \(\int \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx\) where \(Q(x)\) has non-repeated linear factors

blocks.title: Example 40
steps:
Given: \(\int \frac{3x - 2}{x(x - 1)(x - 2)}\,dx\).
To find: the integral.
Method: Case-I. The denominator has three different linear factors \(x\), \(x - 1\), \(x - 2\) and the fraction is proper (degree 1 < degree 3). Split it into three simple fractions, each of which integrates to a logarithm.

Write the partial fractions
\[\dfrac{3x - 2}{x(x - 1)(x - 2)} = \dfrac{A}{x} + \dfrac{B}{x - 1} + \dfrac{C}{x - 2}\]
Why: One unknown constant over each non-repeated linear factor.

Multiply both sides by \(x(x - 1)(x - 2)\)
\[3x - 2 = A(x - 1)(x - 2) + Bx(x - 2)\]
\[+\, Cx(x - 1) \quad (1)\]
Why: This clears the fractions. (1) is an identity, true for every value of \(x\).

Put \(x = 0\) in (1)
\[3(0) - 2 = A(0 - 1)(0 - 2)\]
\[-2 = 2A \;\Rightarrow\; A = -1\]
Why: At \(x = 0\) the \(B\) and \(C\) terms contain the factor \(x = 0\) and vanish.

Put \(x = 1\) in (1)
\[3(1) - 2 = B(1)(1 - 2)\]
\[1 = -B \;\Rightarrow\; B = -1\]
Why: At \(x = 1\) the \(A\) and \(C\) terms contain \(x - 1 = 0\).

Put \(x = 2\) in (1)
\[3(2) - 2 = C(2)(2 - 1)\]
\[4 = 2C \;\Rightarrow\; C = 2\]
Why: At \(x = 2\) the \(A\) and \(B\) terms contain \(x - 2 = 0\).

Integrate term by term
\[\int \left[\dfrac{-1}{x} + \dfrac{-1}{x - 1} + \dfrac{2}{x - 2}\right]dx\]
\[= -\int \dfrac{dx}{x} - \int \dfrac{dx}{x - 1} + 2\int \dfrac{dx}{x - 2}\]
\[= -\ln|x| - \ln|x - 1| + 2\ln|x - 2| + C\]
Why: \(\int \frac{dx}{x - a} = \ln|x - a|\), because the numerator 1 is the derivative of \(x - a\). (Here the book uses capital \(C\) for the constant of integration.)

Check
\[-(x - 1)(x - 2) - x(x - 2) + 2x(x - 1)\]
\[= -x^2 + 3x - 2 - x^2 + 2x + 2x^2 - 2x\]
\[= 3x - 2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Putting the constants back into the right side of (1) gives the numerator \(3x - 2\).

blocks.title: Case-II
blocks.text: Integration of \(\int \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx\) where \(Q(x)\) has repeated linear factors:

blocks.title: Example 41
steps:
Given: \(\int \frac{6x - 10}{(x + 1)(x - 3)^2}\,dx\).
To find: the integral.
Method: Case-II. The factor \(x - 3\) is repeated (squared), so it needs two fractions, one with \(x - 3\) and one with \((x - 3)^2\). Roots give two constants; comparing coefficients gives the third.

Write the partial fractions
\[\dfrac{6x - 10}{(x + 1)(x - 3)^2} = \dfrac{A}{x + 1} + \dfrac{B}{x - 3} + \dfrac{C}{(x - 3)^2}\]
Why: One fraction for \(x + 1\) and one for each power of the repeated factor.

Multiply both sides by \((x + 1)(x - 3)^2\)
\[6x - 10 = A(x - 3)^2 + B(x + 1)(x - 3)\]
\[+\, C(x + 1) \quad (1)\]
\[0\cdot x^2 + 6x - 10 = A(x^2 - 6x + 9)\]
\[+\, B(x^2 - 2x - 3) + C(x + 1) \quad (2)\]
Why: (2) is (1) with the brackets opened; the left side has no \(x^2\) term, so its \(x^2\) coefficient is 0.

Put \(x = 3\) in (1)
\[6(3) - 10 = C(3 + 1)\]
\[8 = 4C \;\Rightarrow\; C = 2\]
Why: \(x - 3 = 0\) removes the \(A\) and \(B\) terms.

Compare the coefficients of \(x^2\) in (2)
\[A + B = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; B = -A = 1\]
Why: No value of \(x\) removes both \(A\) and \(C\) at once, so \(B\) comes from comparing coefficients.

Integrate term by term
\[\int \left[\dfrac{-1}{x + 1} + \dfrac{1}{x - 3} + \dfrac{2}{(x - 3)^2}\right]dx\]
\[= -\ln|x + 1| + \ln|x - 3| + 2\,\dfrac{(x - 3)^{-2+1}}{-2+1} + c\]
Why: The last term is \(2(x - 3)^{-2}\); use the power rule \(\int (x - a)^n\,dx = \frac{(x - a)^{n+1}}{n + 1}\).

Simplify
\[= \ln|x - 3| - \ln|x + 1| + 2\,\dfrac{(x - 3)^{-1}}{-1} + c\]
\[= \ln\left|\dfrac{x - 3}{x + 1}\right| - \dfrac{2}{x - 3} + c\]
Why: \(\ln|p| - \ln|q| = \ln\left|\frac{p}{q}\right|\) and \((x - 3)^{-1} = \frac{1}{x - 3}\).

Check (constant term of (2))
\[9A - 3B + C = -9 - 3 + 2 = -10 \;\checkmark\]
Why: The constant term on the left of (2) is \(-10\); the three constants reproduce it.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does a repeated factor need two fractions? With only \(\frac{C}{(x - 3)^2}\), the factor \((x - 3)\) can only appear in the combined denominator as \((x - 3)^2\), and the numerator \(6x - 10\) cannot be produced. The fraction \(\frac{B}{x - 3}\) supplies the missing freedom. In general \((x - a)^k\) needs \(k\) fractions.

blocks.title: Case-III
blocks.text: Integration of \(\int \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx\) where \(Q(x)\) has at least one non-repeated irreducible quadratic factor.

blocks.title: Example 42
steps:
Given: \(\int \frac{5x^2 + 3x + 2}{(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)}\,dx\).
To find: the integral.
Method: Case-III. \(x + 1\) is linear; \(x^2 + 1\) is an irreducible quadratic (it has no real roots), so its numerator must be linear, \(Bx + C\).

Write the partial fractions
\[\dfrac{5x^2 + 3x + 2}{(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{A}{x + 1} + \dfrac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 1}\]
Why: The book's solution prints the left side here (and again twice below) as \(\frac{5x + 3x + 2}{(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)}\); the numerator is \(5x^2 + 3x + 2\), as in the question.

Multiply both sides by \((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)\)
\[5x^2 + 3x + 2 = A(x^2 + 1)\]
\[+\, (Bx + C)(x + 1) \quad (1)\]
Why: This clears the fractions.

Expand (1) and compare coefficients
\[5x^2 + 3x + 2 = (A + B)x^2 + (B + C)x + (C + A)\]
\[x^2:\ 5 = A + B = 2 + B \;\Rightarrow\; B = 3\]
\[\text{constants}:\ 2 = A + C = C + 2 \;\Rightarrow\; C = 0\]
Why: \(x^2 + 1\) has no real root, so \(B\) and \(C\) come from equating coefficients. (The \(x\) coefficients agree: \(B + C = 3\).)

The integrand becomes
\[\dfrac{5x^2 + 3x + 2}{(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{2}{x + 1} + \dfrac{3x + 0}{x^2 + 1}\]
Why: Put \(A = 2\), \(B = 3\), \(C = 0\).

Integrate
\[= 2\int \dfrac{dx}{x + 1} + \dfrac{3}{2}\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx\]
\[= 2\ln|x + 1| + \dfrac{3}{2}\ln|x^2 + 1| + c\]
\[= 2\ln|x + 1| + \dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2 + 1) + c\]
Why: Multiply and divide by 2 so that the numerator \(2x\) is the derivative of \(x^2 + 1\). The modulus can be dropped because \(x^2 + 1 > 0\).

Check
\[2(x^2 + 1) + 3x(x + 1) = 5x^2 + 3x + 2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: The partial fractions add back to the integrand.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the solution of Example 42 the book prints the integrand three times as \(\frac{5x + 3x + 2}{(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)}\). The numerator must be \(5x^2 + 3x + 2\), as in the question and in equation (1); the working and the answer use the correct \(5x^2 + 3x + 2\).

blocks.title: Case-IV
blocks.text: Integration of \(\int \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx\) where \(Q(x)\) has repeated irreducible quadratic factors:

blocks.title: Example 43
steps:
Given: \(\int \frac{x^3 + 2x + 1}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx\).
To find: the integral.
Method: Case-IV. The irreducible factor \(x^2 + 1\) is repeated. The book finds the partial fractions by splitting the numerator with \(x^2 + 1\) in mind, then uses \(x = \tan\theta\) for the last integral.

Split the numerator
\[x^3 + 2x + 1 = x^3 + x + x + 1\]
\[= x(x^2 + 1) + x + 1\]
Why: Taking \(x\) out of \(x^3 + x\) creates a factor \(x^2 + 1\) that cancels with the denominator.

Partial fractions
\[\dfrac{x(x^2 + 1) + x + 1}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1} + \dfrac{x + 1}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\]
\[= \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1} + \dfrac{x}{(x^2 + 1)^2} + \dfrac{1}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\]
Why: This is the Case-IV form \(\frac{Ax + B}{x^2 + 1} + \frac{Cx + D}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\) with \(A = 1\), \(B = 0\), \(C = 1\), \(D = 1\).

Integrate the first two parts
\[\dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx + \dfrac{1}{2}\int (x^2 + 1)^{-2}(2x)\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(x^2 + 1)^{-1}}{-1}\]
\[+ \int \dfrac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)^2} \quad (1)\]
Why: In both parts \(2x\) is the derivative of \(x^2 + 1\): the first gives a logarithm, the second the power rule.

For \(\int \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\) put \(x = \tan\theta\)
\[dx = \sec^2\theta\,d\theta\]
\[\int \dfrac{\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{(\tan^2\theta + 1)^2} = \int \dfrac{\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{(\sec^2\theta)^2}\]
\[= \int \dfrac{d\theta}{\sec^2\theta} = \int \cos^2\theta\,d\theta\]
Why: \(1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\) turns the denominator into a single power of \(\sec\theta\).

Integrate \(\cos^2\theta\)
\[= \int \dfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\,d\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\theta + \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta\right]\]
Why: \(\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\).

Return to \(x\)
\[\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sec^2\theta}\]
\[= \dfrac{\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2}\]
\[\int \dfrac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1} x + \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2}\right]\]
Why: Multiply and divide by \(\cos\theta\) to reach \(\tan\theta\), then use \(\tan\theta = x\), \(\theta = \tan^{-1} x\). The book prints the middle fraction as \(\frac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos}\): the denominator must be \(\cos\theta\).

Put this into (1)
\[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 1) - \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1}\]
\[+ \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} x + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{x}{1 + x^2} + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} x + \dfrac{x - 1}{2(x^2 + 1)} + c\]
Why: The two fractions have the same denominator \(2(x^2 + 1)\), so \(\frac{x}{2(x^2 + 1)} - \frac{1}{2(x^2 + 1)} = \frac{x - 1}{2(x^2 + 1)}\).

Check (differentiate the answer)
\[\dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1} + \dfrac{1}{2(x^2 + 1)} + \dfrac{(x^2 + 1) - 2x(x - 1)}{2(x^2 + 1)^2}\]
\[= \dfrac{2x^3 + 2x + x^2 + 1 - x^2 + 2x + 1}{2(x^2 + 1)^2}\]
\[= \dfrac{x^3 + 2x + 1}{(x^2 + 1)^2} \;\checkmark\]
Why: The derivative of the answer is the integrand.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 43 the book prints \(\frac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos}\) with the angle missing in the denominator. It should be \(\frac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\) (multiply and divide \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\) by \(\cos\theta\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The integral \(\int \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} x + \frac{x}{2(x^2 + 1)} + c\) found in Example 43 appears again in every Case-IV question (Exercise 3.4, Q13 and Q15). With \(x^2 + a^2\) in place of \(x^2 + 1\), the same idea uses \(x = a\tan\theta\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Partial fractions apply to a proper fraction; if \(\deg P \ge \deg Q\), divide first.
2. Factorise \(Q(x)\) completely: linear factors and irreducible quadratics (\(b^2 - 4ac < 0\)).
3. Non-repeated linear factor: \(\frac{A}{x - a}\). Repeated \((x - a)^k\): \(k\) fractions with powers \(1, \ldots, k\).
4. Irreducible quadratic factor: linear numerator \(\frac{Ax + B}{x^2 + bx + c}\); repeated quadratics need one such fraction for each power.
5. Constants: put roots first, then compare coefficients; check by adding the fractions back.
6. Linear parts integrate to \(\ln\), squared parts by the power rule, quadratic parts to \(\ln\) plus \(\tan^{-1}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Splitting an improper fraction without dividing first (e.g. \(\frac{x^3 + 2x^2 - x - 1}{x^2 - 1}\)).
2. Writing only \(\frac{C}{(x - 3)^2}\) for a repeated factor and forgetting \(\frac{B}{x - 3}\).
3. Writing a constant \(\frac{B}{x^2 + 1}\) over a quadratic factor instead of \(\frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 1}\).
4. Forgetting \(\frac{1}{a}\): \(\int \frac{dx}{4 - 3x} = -\frac{1}{3}\ln|4 - 3x|\), not \(\ln|4 - 3x|\).
5. Integrating \(\frac{1}{(x - 3)^2}\) as a logarithm; it is \(-\frac{1}{x - 3}\).
